steps.prompt: What's the ONE thing an AI PM does that nobody else on the team can?
steps.sub: You're not here to become an ML engineer. You're here to stand in the middle — translating between business value, user need, and what's technically possible — so the team makes good bets. By the end you'll think in the 5 shifts that hit every product the moment it LEARNS from data instead of following rules you wrote.

steps.prompt: Where does an AI PM's unique value actually come from?
steps.sub: Pick the truest one, then check.

options.t: Writing the model code so engineers don't have to.
Translating between business value, user need, and what's technically/data-wise POSSIBLE — so the team bets well.
Knowing more ML math than the data scientists.

steps.why: The AI PM sits at the intersection of three forces — what's worth money (business), what people actually need (user), and what the data and models can realistically do (feasibility). You don't out-code the engineers or out-math the scientists. You make the bets nobody else is positioned to make, and you talk credibly to ML/data teams. That translation IS the job.
hints: It's a position, not a skill you out-compete a specialist on.
Three circles overlap: business, user, feasibility. You live in the overlap.

steps.prompt: The 5 shifts when a product LEARNS instead of following your rules.
steps.sub: Tap each card. These are what change the moment ML enters the product.

cards.b: It's right MOST of the time, not every time. You ship a percentage and DESIGN for the wrong %. Acharya the tutor will sometimes answer wrong — the product is the safety net around that, not the model alone.

cards.h: 2 · Data is raw material, moat, AND risk
cards.b: No good data, no product. Great proprietary data is your moat. Bad/biased/illegal data is your biggest liability. The data strategy IS the product strategy.
A model optimizes EXACTLY what you measure — not what you meant. Pick the metric carelessly and you ship the wrong product perfectly. This is the central failure mode.

cards.h: 4 · Feasibility is uncertain until you build
cards.b: Nobody can promise it'll work upfront. You de-risk with spikes, baselines, and quick experiments — not guarantees. 'Can we even do this?' is answered by building, fast and cheap.

cards.h: 5 · The human loop never fully closes
cards.b: Eval, monitoring, drift, fairness, privacy — these are ongoing OPERATIONS, not a launch checklist you tick once. The product is alive after ship; the world changes and the model goes stale.

steps.prompt: Acharya, our AI tutor, gives a wrong answer to 1 student in 20. The team panics: 'the model is broken!' What's the AI PM's mindset?
steps.sub: Which response shows you've internalized shift #1?

options.t: Agreed — a wrong answer means the model failed. Block launch until it's 100% correct.
It's probabilistic — it's right most of the time. The real job is designing for the wrong 5%: show sources, let students flag, add a 'not sure' path.
Ignore it — 1 in 20 is rare enough that students won't notice.

steps.why: Demanding 100% means you'll never ship — learning systems are probabilistic by nature. And ignoring the 5% is how you lose trust. The mature move is to accept the wrong percentage exists and build the product AROUND it: confidence signals, sources, a feedback button, graceful 'I'm not sure' answers. You ship the right %, and you design for the wrong one.
hints: 100% correct is not on the menu for a learning system. So what IS the job?
Shift #1 said: ship the right %, and DESIGN for the wrong %.

steps.prompt: Each product question below belongs to one of the 5 shifts. Sort them.
steps.sub: Tap a question, then the shift it's really probing.

items.t: 'What happens when the model is confidently wrong, and how do users recover?'
'Do we have the legal right to use this data, and is it representative of our real users?'
'If we optimize for watch-time, will it start recommending junk that just keeps people scrolling?'
'Who watches for drift and fairness 3 months after launch, and how often?'
'Our proprietary lesson data — is THAT actually our moat versus a competitor?'
'We hit our accuracy number but users hate it — did we measure the wrong thing?'

hints: Match the WORRY in each question to the shift that names that worry.
Anything about legal/representative/moat → data. Anything about 'optimized the wrong number' → metric.

steps.prompt: A team builds a job-recommender and tells the model: maximize click-through. It learns to recommend mostly clickbait gigs. What went wrong?
steps.sub: This is the most common AI-product failure. Name it.

options.t: The model was too small — buy more GPUs.
The metric defined the behaviour: it optimized clicks EXACTLY, not 'good jobs for this user'. The target was wrong, so the product is wrong.
Users behaved unexpectedly — nothing the team could have done.

steps.why: This is shift #3, the central failure mode. The model did its job perfectly — it maximized what you measured. You measured clicks; you got clicks, even on junk. The model has no idea you 'meant' good job matches. The AI PM's most important upstream decision is choosing a metric that actually proxies the outcome you want (e.g. applications + interviews + good fit, not raw clicks).
hints: The model didn't disobey — it obeyed too well. Obeyed WHAT?
Shift #3: a model optimizes exactly what you measure.

steps.prompt: Put the AIPM loop in order — from raw problem to a feedback flywheel.
steps.sub: Tap the steps in the order a disciplined AI PM runs them.
chips: Define the problem & the outcome you want
Ask: is AI even the right tool here?
Check the data — available, legal, representative?
Build a baseline (often non-ML) to beat
Online eval — A/B test on real users
Feed results back into the data
hints: Two gates come BEFORE you touch a model: is AI right, and is the data OK?
Always set a baseline before the model — so offline eval has something to beat. Online (A/B) comes after offline.

steps.prompt: Before training anything, why does a sharp AI PM insist on a baseline — often a dumb non-ML rule?
steps.sub: We did this with the drone RL policy too. Why bother?

options.t: To pad the timeline so the project looks bigger.
So 'is the fancy model actually worth it?' has an answer — and to de-risk feasibility cheaply before committing.
Baselines are just tradition; they don't really change decisions.

steps.why: A baseline gives offline eval a number to beat and answers feasibility fast and cheap (shift #4). If a one-line heuristic ('recommend most-popular') already gets you 80% of the value, a heavy model may not be worth its cost and risk. With the drone policy, a simple controller is the bar the learned policy has to clearly beat — otherwise why take on a black box? Baselines turn 'we think AI helps' into 'AI beats the baseline by X'.
hints: What does offline eval compare the model AGAINST?
Shift #4: you de-risk feasibility with spikes and baselines, not promises.

steps.prompt: Myth-check the AI PM mindset — true or false?

statements.t: An AI PM's job is to write the model so they don't depend on ML engineers.
statements.why: No — the job is to translate between business, user, and feasibility and talk credibly to ML/data teams, not to replace them.

statements.t: A learning product is probabilistic — you ship the right % and design for the wrong %.
statements.why: Yes — that's shift #1. 100% correct isn't on the menu; the product is the safety net around the wrong percentage.

statements.t: Once the metric is set, the model will optimize what you MEANT, not just what you measured.
statements.why: False — and it's the central failure mode. It optimizes exactly what you measure. Clickbait happens when clicks were the metric.

statements.t: Eval, drift-monitoring, fairness and privacy are ongoing operations, not a one-time launch checklist.
statements.why: Yes — shift #5. The world shifts after launch, models go stale, so the human loop never fully closes.

hints: Two of these describe the SHIFTS correctly; two are tempting traps.
The model optimizes what you MEASURE, not what you mean — that flips one statement to false.

steps.sub: Not graded. Tying this to your real work is what makes it stick.

fields.label: What product or feature do you (or want to) work on where ML could learn from data?
fields.ph: e.g. support-ticket routing, a recommender, a tutor like Acharya

fields.label: For that product, name the metric you'd optimize — and one way it could backfire (shift #3):
fields.ph: e.g. optimize 'replies sent' → agents close tickets without solving them

steps.prompt: Lock it in: tap EVERY statement that's part of the AI PM mindset.
chips: Translate between business value, user need, and what's technically possible
Learning products are probabilistic — design for the wrong %
The data strategy IS the product strategy
A model optimizes exactly what you measure
De-risk feasibility with baselines and spikes, not guarantees
Eval and monitoring end at launch — it's a one-time checklist
steps.why: The first five ARE the mindset: you live in the business/user/feasibility overlap; learning systems are probabilistic; data strategy is product strategy; the metric defines behaviour; and feasibility gets de-risked by building. The last is false — eval, drift, fairness and privacy are ongoing operations (shift #5), not something you tick once and forget.
